title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Open-source governance, risk, and compliance Risk and compliance people actually keep current RiskWren is one connected register of what an organization has, what could go wrong, what it must comply with, what it does about both, and the proof. It is built first for the security team: frameworks, assessments, findings, and exceptions are the path it gets right before anything else. Get started Try the demo Source on GitHub

title: Overview
heading: Test once, satisfy many
text: A control is described once, mapped to every requirement it answers, and tested once. The result shows in every framework and every scope that relies on it.

title: Overview
heading: Worked out, never typed in
text: Readiness comes from tests and evidence that still count. Saying a control is in place never makes it verified, and what was verified decays by itself.

title: Overview
heading: Nobody marks their own work
text: A second person confirms a test result, the closure of an issue, and an exception. The server refuses anything else, whatever the role.

title: Overview
heading: Passive by design
text: No scanners, collectors, or agents, and no access to anything else on the network. It records what people know and decide. Readiness

title: Overview
heading: Where you stand against a framework, with the reason
text: A scope is a boundary held to one or more frameworks. Each requirement that applies in it is in exactly one of six states: verified, in place, excepted, planned, gap, or failing. Each control that answers it carries a sentence saying how it came to be there. When a central team's control fails a test, every scope that inherits it shows the failure the same day. How readiness is worked out Assessments

title: Overview
heading: A result counts when a second person confirms it
text: An assessment plans a test for each control a scope does itself. Nobody records or reviews a result for a control they own, and whoever recorded a result cannot confirm it. Once confirmed, the result becomes the control's rating, moves every requirement the control answers in every scope that relies on it, and moves the residual rating suggested for every risk it reduces. Assessments and tests Issues

title: Overview
heading: Every finding in one register, each with a date
text: A failed test opens an issue for the control's owners without anyone asking. Penetration tests, audits, incidents, and gaps go in the same register. Severity sets the date. Moving it needs a reason and stays on the record. An issue closes only when someone who does not own it confirms it was put right. Issues, from raised to closed Exceptions

title: Overview
heading: Exceptions that end by themselves
text: When a requirement cannot be met yet, the honest answer is an exception: why, what is done meanwhile, and the dates it runs between. Whoever asked does not decide. While it is in force the requirement shows as excepted, with the state underneath beside it. The day after it ends, that state is back. Nothing has to run for that to happen. Asking, deciding, and what follows Incidents

title: Overview
heading: Something went wrong: reported in a minute, handled on the record
text: Anyone signed in reports an incident, a near miss, or a concern in one short form. Where the organization opens it, anyone can without giving a name, and follows it up with a code. Triage names the systems, information, and third parties involved, and who handles it; the reporter sees where it stands, not the handling. What it taught stays: the risks it realized, the controls that failed or held, and what it cost, shown on each risk and control. A sensitive case is kept to those named on it, and nobody else learns it exists. Incidents Breach assessment

title: Overview
heading: Must we notify anyone, and by when?
text: An incident involving protected information is assessed on its factors, and what follows is worked out from the rules that apply: the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, the FTC Safeguards Rule, DFARS 252.204-7012, a state's law, or a contract. Each says to whom, within how long, and by what day, from the moment the incident was discovered. Each notification is recorded as it is sent, and what is still due waits on the handler's home page until it is. Breach assessment Connections

title: Overview
heading: What is this connected to?
text: In an incident or a review the questions are always the same: what does this system support, which scopes is it in, what controls stand in front of it, and what is already known to be wrong with them. Every record opens to a picture of what it is joined to, with a list beside it that says the same in full. All of it works from the keyboard. Connections Risk

title: Overview
heading: Ratings you can read, decided by named people
text: Likelihood and impact have five levels, each with a written definition. Inherent, residual, and target ratings are judgments by named people, with reasons. The controls linked to a risk suggest a residual rating, and the suggestion opens to the arithmetic behind it. When a test moves it past the rating on record, the risk is flagged and its owner is asked to assess again. What the controls suggest Home

title: Overview
heading: One page of what each person owes
text: Most people who own a risk, a control, or an action are not risk professionals. Home lists what is theirs to do, each item a short task: a test to record, a result to confirm, an issue to put right, an exception about to end. A security leader's Home starts with the figures that cannot wait, such as controls failing a test and issues past their date, then the decisions that are theirs to make. Home Keeping watch

title: Overview
heading: Ask the owners, and see who has answered
text: A campaign asks every control owner to attest, every risk owner to look again, or for a named piece of evidence, by a date. Its page shows who has answered, unit by unit, and reminds those who have not. What an owner says of a control is shown apart from its rating. It never makes a requirement verified, and it takes one out of verified when the owner says the control no longer operates. Campaigns Early warning

title: Overview
heading: A number that warns before the risk arrives
text: An indicator is a number someone already reads: servers patched within thirty days, days to remove a leaver's access. Give it a warning level and a limit, and record what it stands at. Past the limit, its owners and the owners of every risk it warns of are told, and those risks are marked for another look. Nothing is fetched: a person reads the number and records it. Indicators The program

title: Overview
heading: See what a change would do before you make it
text: The matrix, appetite, and the review cadences are edited in the app. A change is held as a draft, and a preview lists every open risk whose rating, standing, or next review would move. The preview is the change itself, made and undone, so publishing changes exactly the risks it listed. Judgments already made keep the rating they were given. Shape the program Risk analysis

title: Overview
heading: Each thing against each threat, with a report
text: A risk analysis takes what is in a scope and a list of threats, and asks of each pair whether it applies. The answer is that it does not, that a risk on the register covers it, or that a risk is raised for the thing's owner. It closes when every question has an answer. What it considered, what was decided, and why stay on record as its report. Risk analyses Resilience

title: Overview
heading: What the organization cannot afford to lose, and whether it can get it back
text: A process's business impact says how its loss hurts over time, how soon it must be back, and how much information it can lose. Everything it relies on (its systems, services, and sites, and the third parties that perform it) is checked against that, and every shortfall is listed. Continuity plans say what they restore and whom to call, print or download as one file for when the systems are down, and are exercised, with findings that become issues. Business impact and recovery Policies

title: Overview
heading: Approved by named people, and never altered
text: A policy, standard, procedure, or guideline is written here, linked to where it is kept, or attached as a file. A new version goes to the people who must approve it, none of whom wrote it, and is published once every one of them has. A published version is never changed. Its fingerprint is in the history, and riskwren verify checks it. Any two versions compare side by side, and each document comes up for review on a cadence. Policies Acknowledgment

title: Overview
heading: Read by the people it applies to, and acknowledged
text: Everyone has a library of the documents that apply to them, readable on a phone. A document that asks to be acknowledged stays on each person's Home until they have; a new version asks again, unless its author says the change does not need it. Who has and who has not is shown by unit and by person, and a campaign chases the rest by a date. Acknowledgment Agreements

title: Overview
heading: What you promised others, with its dates
text: An award, a data use agreement, a business associate agreement: each with its parties, its dates, and its notice period. The terms it imposes reach every scope that holds what it covers, which says why it holds them. Its owners are told before the last day to give notice and before it ends. One that has ended stays open until it is renewed or closed. Agreements Framework updates

title: Overview
heading: A new version beside the old, and what changed
text: A framework's new version is loaded beside the one in use, and nothing that uses the old one changes. What changed is listed by code, with the words that differ, and where the publisher says each withdrawn requirement went. A scope moves when its keepers say so, taking its decisions and exceptions with it where the code is unchanged. Framework versions Internal audit

title: Overview
heading: Internal audit on the same record, with its independence kept
text: The universe ranks everything worth auditing from the register, with its working shown. Engagements are planned, approved, and carried out with workpapers signed off by someone other than their preparer, and until the report is issued, the work is the audit team's alone. Findings land in the one issue register, with management's action plan, and internal audit confirms them closed. An outside auditor can be given one engagement, read-only, with every look recorded. Internal audit Leadership reports

title: Overview
heading: A report to leadership that can be shown to be the one given
text: The top risks and how each moved since the last report, appetite, posture by framework, the suppliers with most at stake, the measures against last time, and what is overdue, with the issuer's own summary. Issued, it is frozen with a fingerprint the history records. It reopens exactly as it was, whatever has happened since, and says whether it still verifies. Leadership reports Risk in numbers

title: Overview
heading: What a year of a risk could cost, and how sure that is
text: For the risks worth a figure, how often a year and what each time costs, as ranges with what they assume. A simulation of ten thousand years says the average, the loss exceeded one year in ten, and the chance of passing each figure, the same every time it is run. A scenario adds up the risks it touches, and every risk's bow-tie shows which controls stand before the event and which after. Estimates in ranges Committees

title: Overview
heading: A committee's decision, on the record it was about
text: A session's agenda is drawn from the register: the risks above appetite, an exception, a policy waiting for approval. The decision on each item is recorded with it, shows on the record it was about, and is told to that record's owners. Strategic objectives connect the register to the plan: each lists exactly the risks that threaten it. Committee sessions Third parties

title: Overview
heading: Every supplier tiered by your own rules, with the reasons
text: A supplier's services say what it reaches and handles. A few questions, answered mostly from the inventory, give its tier by the program's rules, and every reason that applied is shown. The tier is a judgment by a named person: a different one from the rules' needs a reason, and both are kept. The tier sets how often the supplier is reviewed. Tiering Due diligence

title: Overview
heading: A security questionnaire, without giving anyone an account
text: The questionnaire the tier names goes to the supplier's contact through a link that expires. Only a digest of it is kept, it travels where no server logs it, and it opens that one form and nothing else. The answers that are concerns are listed first, and the reviewer records what was concluded. A concern becomes a finding, followed up with the supplier's own people. Due diligence Assurance

title: Overview
heading: What a SOC 2 report actually covers
text: Reports and certificates are kept with their period and expiry, and read for what they cover: the services in scope and those not, the carve-outs, the exceptions noted. What a report leaves to the organization is joined to the control that does it, and that control's page says a supplier's assurance leans on it. Reviewing a report Coverage

title: Overview
heading: A stop wherever the paper is missing
text: The program says which agreements shared information needs: a business associate agreement for patient records handled for you, a data use agreement for controlled-access data. Where information is shared and no such agreement with that supplier covers it, the information, the supplier, and the service each show a stop, until one does. Coverage Production

title: Overview
heading: From a laptop to production, and told what stands in the way
text: It runs as a container with PostgreSQL or as a locked-down service, backs up to one file that restores into either database, and starts from a program written for a research institute, an academic medical center, a university, or a nonprofit. riskwren doctor --production and the operations page say what is not yet ready. Other systems come in with tokens that act as a role, never as a person, and hear what happens through signed webhooks that carry references, never contents. It was reviewed against the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard at level 2. Deployment

title: Overview
heading: Frameworks as published
text: NIST CSF 2.0, SP 800-53 Rev. 5 with its baselines, SP 800-171 Rev. 3, and the HIPAA Security Rule arrive loaded, and SP 800-53 Rev. 4 is there for programs that still name it. An agreement's terms or an internal standard is entered as a framework of your own.

title: Overview
heading: Inherited controls
text: A central team runs backup and identity once. Other scopes inherit those controls, and see a failure the day the provider's test finds it.

title: Overview
heading: Evidence that stops counting
text: Evidence is collected once and attached to everything it supports. Past its date it stays on the record and counts toward nothing.

title: Overview
heading: Working on the first day
text: A risk taxonomy, a scoring method, 57 common risks, and 75 common controls come with a new installation. The security controls among them arrive mapped to about three quarters of each framework.

title: Overview
heading: A history that holds
text: Every change is in an append-only, hash-chained log, with who made it. An auditor reads everything and changes nothing.

title: Overview
heading: Rating and standing
text: How much is at stake, and whether it is in order, are always two signals. Neither is told by color alone.

title: Overview
heading: In and out
text: Every list exports as CSV or JSON. Records come in from a spreadsheet, with a dry run that reports every problem by row.

title: Overview
heading: Who sees what
text: Roles are held over units. A figure never counts a record its reader could not open, and evidence is more closely held than the register.

title: Overview
heading: Sign in your way
text: Local accounts out of the box. Optional single sign-on by OpenID Connect, built to work with Microsoft Entra ID, with roles and units taken from the provider.

title: Overview
heading: It knows what is due
text: Whoever a thing is waiting on is reminded before its date and when it passes, then their steward, then their leader. Email is optional.

title: Overview
heading: Found, and kept in order
text: One search across every kind of record, saved views of any list, what each record is missing, and likely duplicates. When someone leaves, nothing is left without an owner.

title: Overview
heading: Open and yours
text: Apache 2.0 with no paid edition. SQLite on a laptop or PostgreSQL on a server, five runtime dependencies, and your own name and colors.

title: Getting started
heading: Getting started
text: Getting started This guide takes you from nothing to a running RiskWren that your organization can sign in to. It is for whoever installs it and sets it up. Allow about fifteen minutes. If you only want to look around first, skip to Explore the demo organization .

title: Getting started
heading: What you need
text: uv , which provides the right Python (3.12 or later). A copy of this repository. Every command in these guides is run through uv run riskwren … from the repository directory. The full list is in the command reference .

title: Getting started
heading: Install
text: uv sync

title: Getting started
heading: Set up the installation
text: uv run riskwren init init does five things: Writes riskwren.toml , the deployment settings, in the current directory. Creates the data home, ./var , which holds everything that is not in the database. Creates the database. With no other setting, this is a SQLite file inside the data home. Loads the default program: nine families of risk with an appetite for each, a scoring method with defined scales, review cadences, the table of who may accept what, a library of 57 common risks, a library of 75 common controls, and four public frameworks (the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, and the HIPAA Security Rule) with the common controls already mapped

title: Getting started
heading: Check it
text: uv run riskwren doctor doctor checks the configuration, the data home, that the database answers, that its schema is the one this version expects, that the database still refuses changes to the history, and that the history verifies. It exits with 1 if anything must be fixed.

title: Getting started
heading: Run it
text: uv run riskwren serve The server prints its address, by default http://127.0.0.1:8000 . Use --port to pick another port. serve refuses to start in three cases, and says what to do in each: It says Do this The database schema is behind uv run riskwren db upgrade There is no administrator yet uv run riskwren users add you@example.org --name "Your Name" --role admin The port is already in use Stop what is using it, or pass --port As installed, RiskWren listens only on the machine it runs on. To put it in front of other people, read Configuration first.

title: Getting started
heading: Sign in for the first time
text: Open the address in a browser and sign in with the email address and password you gave init . RiskWren signs in with local accounts: an email address and a password that it keeps. Nothing else has to be installed or connected. Signing in with your organization's identity provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID, is optional and can be added at any time: see Single sign-on . Five failed attempts within fifteen minutes stop sign-in for that account from that address for a few minutes. A sign-in ends after 12 hours without activity, and after 7 days in any case. Both are settings . To change your password, open the account menu at the top right and choose Your account . Changing it signs out your o

title: Getting started
heading: Set up the organization
text: The administrator account sets the installation up. It does not assess or accept risk: that belongs to the roles below, and an administrator who also does that work is given a second role.

title: Getting started
heading: Units
text: Admin → Units holds the organization as a hierarchy of any depth: divisions, departments, labs, cores, clinics, offices. Every record belongs to a unit, roles can be limited to a unit and everything beneath it, and figures roll up the tree. Give each unit a short code; imports and the command line refer to units by it.

title: Getting started
heading: People and roles
text: Admin → People adds accounts and gives them roles. A person with no role is a member: they see what they are named on, and their own unit's register if the program allows it. Role What it is for Manager The risk and compliance team. Edits any record, shapes the program, reads everything. Can be limited to a unit Assessor Assesses risks and rates controls they do not own. Can be limited to a unit Auditor Reads everything, including the full history, and changes nothing Leader Leads a unit. Sees it and everything beneath it, and may accept risk in it up to a limit set on the role Steward Keeps a unit's records: adds and edits its processes, systems, third parties, risks, and controls Admin Acc

title: Getting started
heading: Import units and people
text: Both screens take a CSV file, which is the quick way to load an organization. Each import can be run dry first and reports every problem by row, so nothing is half-loaded. The import dialog shows the columns it expects.

title: Getting started
heading: Appearance
text: Admin → Appearance sets the product's name, your organization's name, a logo, an accent color, the default palette, and how ratings are colored. See Running the program .

title: Adopting RiskWren
heading: Adopting RiskWren
text: Adopting RiskWren For an organization deciding whether to use RiskWren, and then putting it into use: what to look at, how to pilot it, what to decide, and how to go live. The program handbook takes over once it is running.

title: Adopting RiskWren
heading: Look at it
text: Build the demo organization on a laptop and sign in as each of its sample people ( Explore the demo organization ). It is a fictional research institute with two years of history, and every screen has something on it. Look at it as the people who would use it: The security leader and the risk manager : the dashboards, the register, the program, and the reports to leadership. A steward and a staff member : what a person who answers for a few things sees, and how little they are asked. The auditor : whether the record can be shown to be what it says it was, on any date. Then read the changelog , which lists what each release does, and the end of the guides' index in the repository ( docs/READM

title: Adopting RiskWren
heading: Pilot it
text: A pilot of six to twelve weeks answers the questions that matter: will the people who must keep it current do so, and does what it shows hold up? Install it as you would for production ( Deployment ), with PostgreSQL, behind your proxy, with backups, but with a starter program and nothing imported yet. Choose a slice of the organization: one division, or the systems in one compliance scope. Large enough to have real risks and real owners; small enough to finish. Do the first month and the first quarter of the handbook for that slice, with its real stewards and owners. Judge it by what the pilot's people did, not by what they said: did owners answer their reminders, did a test result move rea

title: Adopting RiskWren
heading: Decide
text: Before going wider, settle the decisions in Decide first , and these about the installation: Decision Where Who runs the installation, and who is the second administrator Roles; Deployment How people sign in: local accounts, single sign-on, or both Single sign-on Whether to send email, and from what address Email How backups are taken, kept, and tested Back up and restore The look: your names, logos, colors, and words, in the app or fixed in the file Appearance , [branding] Which other systems read from it, and with what token; which are told of events Tokens , webhooks Whether reports may be made without a name Reporting without a name

title: Adopting RiskWren
heading: Go live
text: Run riskwren doctor --production until it has nothing to fix ( Check before going live ). Bring in what you have: units and people, then the inventory, risks, and controls from spreadsheets, each with a dry run that reports every problem by row before anything is loaded ( Import and export ). Widen one division or scope at a time, each with its stewards shown what is theirs. Campaigns do the asking ( Campaigns ). Turn on what reaches people last: email, then reminders' escalation to stewards and leaders, once records have owners who know they are owners.

title: Adopting RiskWren
heading: Keep it current
text: Upgrades come as releases, each with a changelog that says what looks different afterwards. Back up, then upgrade ( Upgrade ). Within 0.x, a release may change the API; the changes are listed under Breaking , and the contract catches them before they ship. Security problems are reported as SECURITY.md says. The application was reviewed against the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard at level 2; the review and what was done about each finding are in the repository's spec/security-review.md . Your program is yours: export it as one file ( riskwren program export ) to keep it under version control or carry it to another installation.

title: The program handbook
heading: The program handbook
text: The program handbook For a risk and compliance team, most often the security office, running its program in RiskWren: what to decide first, what to do in the first months, and the rhythm of a year. The other guides say how each part works; this one says when to use it, and why.

title: The program handbook
heading: Decide first
text: A few decisions shape everything after them. Make them before you enter much, and write them down: each one is a setting you can change later, but records made under one setting are not remade under the next. Decision Where it is set A good start Who runs the program Roles: managers run it, administrators keep the installation Two managers from the security or risk office, and an administrator who is not one of them What the first year covers Your plan, not a setting The systems and processes that hold restricted information, and the frameworks you are already held to The program to start from riskwren init --program The one nearest your organization; adjust it under Admin → Program The unit

title: The program handbook
heading: The first month: the record
text: Units and people. Import them from a spreadsheet ( Import units and people ), or connect single sign-on and let roles come from the identity provider ( Single sign-on ). Name a steward for each unit in the first year's scope. The inventory. Start with what matters most: the critical processes and the systems they rely on, then the third parties and information assets behind them. Link them as you go: relies on , holds , shared with . A record without links is a list; with them it is a picture ( Connections ). Controls. Take the common controls from the library and write what each does here; add your own. Name an owner for each. Map them to your frameworks: the library's controls arrive mappe

title: The program handbook
heading: The first quarter: the evidence
text: Test what matters. An assessment of each scope's key controls, results recorded by someone who does not own the control and confirmed by a second person ( Assessments and tests ). Readiness moves to verified only here. Collect evidence once. Attach each piece to everything it supports, with the date it holds to. It stops counting on its own ( Evidence stops counting ). Put failures right. A failed test opens an issue; an issue has a date from its severity, actions with owners, and is closed by someone who did not fix it ( Issues and exceptions ). What cannot be fixed yet is an exception, decided and dated. Policies. Load the documents you have, link each to the controls it directs and the re

title: The program handbook
heading: The yearly rhythm
text: Once the record is in place, the program is the same work on a calendar. Scheduled work reminds owners before things are due, then their stewards and leaders when they are late ( Reminders ), so the team chases less and reads more. When What Where Every week Triage new incidents and concerns; read what is waiting on home Incidents; Home Every month Issues past their date, exceptions ending, indicators past their limit, evidence about to stop counting The compliance and risk dashboards; Indicators Every quarter The risk committee meets on an agenda drawn from the register; a leadership report is issued and kept as it was given; control owners attest Committee sessions; Leadership reports; Cam

title: The program handbook
heading: Who does what
text: Role In the program Security leader, risk manager (managers) Shape the program, run campaigns and committee sessions, issue leadership reports, decide exceptions within their authority Stewards Keep their unit's records current: inventory, risks, controls, owners Owners of risks, controls, and actions Answer for one thing each, and are reminded when it is due Assessors Test controls, review results, confirm closures, triage incidents Leaders Accept risks within their authority, and read their units' standing Auditors Read everything and change nothing; internal audit plans and works on the same record Administrators Accounts, units, the look, single sign-on, tokens, and the installation Ever

title: The program handbook
heading: What to watch
text: Measures say what they count and open the list behind each figure. Early on, watch coverage: how much of the inventory has owners, risks rated, and controls mapped. Later, watch movement: risks above appetite, issues past their date, controls failing a test, and readiness by scope against each framework. A figure that never moves is a figure nobody is acting on.

title: The register
heading: The register
text: The register This guide is for everyone who owns, assesses, or reads a risk. It covers the inventory, risks and their ratings, controls, what the controls suggest, treatment plans, and acceptance. What the organization is held to, and the proof that it meets it, is in Compliance . RiskWren is one connected register. A system is recorded once and every risk that concerns it points at it. A control is described once and every risk it bears on leans on the same record, with the same rating of how well it works.

title: The register
heading: Home
text: Home is the page for what you owe. Waiting on you lists, most urgent first, the things that need you in particular: an action that is yours, a risk of yours that has not been assessed or is due for review, a risk whose rating is in doubt, a risk that needs a decision, a control of yours to rate, an acceptance you gave that is about to expire, evidence of yours that has stopped counting or soon will, a test you have been asked to do, a result waiting for your review, an issue that is yours to put right, a closure waiting for you to confirm, an exception to decide or one of yours about to end, and, for those who can name a new owner, a record with nobody answering for it. Each item is a link t

title: The register
heading: The inventory
text: The inventory is what the organization has and depends on. It has six kinds of record: Record What it is Reference Process Something the organization does: a service a core provides, a clinical activity, payroll PRC-0001 System What the work runs on: an application, a platform, an instrument, a device, a data store SYS-0001 Third party Who it depends on: suppliers, service providers, collaborators, sponsors, subrecipients TP-0001 Information asset A body of information it holds: what it is, where it is kept, and who it is shared with. The record describes the information and never contains it INF-0001 Service What a third party provides: a hosted application, a maintenance contract, a test s

title: The register
heading: Links
text: A record says what it relies on: From Link To Process relies on System Process is performed by Third party System is supplied by Third party System holds Information asset Process uses Information asset Information asset is shared with Third party Service reaches · handles System · Information asset Process · System relies on · is supplied by Service Third party subcontracts to Another third party Process or system depends on · is part of Another of the same kind A link is made once, from either end, and can be read from both. A lab can say that its work relies on central storage without anyone in central computing doing anything.

title: The register
heading: Business impact and recovery
text: A process's Business impact tab says what the organization cannot afford to lose: how much its loss hurts as time goes on (after four hours, a day, three days, a week, and a month, from negligible to severe), how soon it must be back (its recovery time), how much information it can afford to lose (its recovery point), and the least it needs to run. An analysis is a judgment by a named person and is never edited: analysing again supersedes it, and every one is kept. A system's, a service's, a site's, or a third party's Recovery tab says what it can actually deliver: what it can be restored within, how much information it can lose, and what that rests on (a restore tested on a date, a supplier

title: The register
heading: Continuity plans and exercises
text: A continuity plan says what to do to keep a process going, or to bring it back, when something stops it. It is written as a document of the kind Continuity plan ( Policies ), so it has versions, approval by named people before each is published, owners, and a review date, as any document does. Reports → Continuity plans lists every plan in use, and the processes with a business impact analysis that no plan restores. A plan's page shows the version in force, and, beside it, what is needed to use it: What it restores, soonest first: each process it is said to restore ( Change , by those who keep the plan), how soon it must be back and how much information it can lose, the least it needs, and e

title: The register
heading: Connections
text: Every record has a Connections link beside its name. It opens a picture of everything joined to the record: its links in both directions, the risks that bear on it, the controls that reduce them, the scopes it is in, and the evidence, issues, and exceptions about it. A list beside the picture says the same in full. See Connections .

title: The register
heading: Known elsewhere as
text: A record can carry what it is called in other systems: an asset tag, a contract number, a ticket, an entry in a configuration database. Known elsewhere as → Edit on the record. Search finds a record by any of them, and where the system has an address pattern they are links.

title: The register
heading: Import and export
text: Every list has an Export button. It gives the list as it is filtered, and as much of it as you may see, as a spreadsheet (CSV) or as data (JSON). Taking an export is recorded in the history. A steward or a manager can Import processes, systems, third parties, information assets, risks, and controls from a spreadsheet saved as CSV: Choose the file. RiskWren reads its headings and matches them to fields where the names make it plain. Say which column holds anything it could not match. A unit is given by its code or its name, an owner by their email address, and a choice by its key or by the words you see in the app. Check the file. Every problem is listed with its row. Nothing has been added y

title: The register
heading: Owners
text: Every record names the people who answer for it. An owner is accountable, a delegate acts for the owner day to day, and a contact knows the detail. Owners and delegates may edit the record. When an owner's account is disabled, nothing they answered for is left without an owner. What they alone owned passes to the steward of its unit, who is told, and stays listed as theirs to pass on until someone is named for good. See When someone leaves .

title: The register
heading: History
text: Every record has a History tab: who changed what, when, with each value before and after. Nothing in it can be edited or removed. See The history .

title: The register
heading: Raise a risk
text: Register → Raise a risk. Start from the library when you can, by searching it at the top of the form: it holds 57 common risks, written as a cause, an event, and a consequence, each with its category and the controls commonly used for it. Change the wording to fit; the library is a starting point, not a standard. A risk needs a name, a category, and a unit. Say what it concerns by linking the processes, systems, and third parties involved, so that anyone looking at a system sees the risks that bear on it.

title: The register
heading: Assess it
text: A risk carries up to three ratings, and each is a judgment recorded by a named person with a reason. Rating The question it answers Inherent How much is at stake if the controls did not exist or did not work? Residual How much remains, with the controls as they actually work? Target Where should it be once the plan is done? To assess, choose a likelihood from 1 (rare) to 5 (almost certain) and an impact from 1 to 5 on each dimension that applies: mission, safety, financial, legal, and trust. Every level has a written definition, shown as you choose, so that two people rating the same thing reach the same answer. The overall impact is the highest level on any dimension, and the rating is read

title: The register
heading: Rating and standing
text: These are two different things, and RiskWren always shows them apart. The rating says how much is at stake. The standing says whether the risk is in order. Standing Meaning Within appetite The residual rating is at or below what the organization has said it will live with for this kind of risk Being treated Above appetite, with a plan that is active and on time Accepted Above appetite, and accepted by someone with the authority, until a date Needs a decision Above appetite, and neither treated nor accepted. This is what leaders should look at Not assessed No residual rating yet Closed No longer applies, and kept for the record A critical risk that is accepted is in order. A moderate one in a

title: The register
heading: Reviews
text: Each risk has a next review date, sooner the more is at stake: by default every 3 months for critical, 6 for high, 12 for moderate, and 24 for low. A review is a new residual assessment, even when nothing has changed; say so in the reason. A risk past its date shows as overdue, on its page and on its owner's Home.

title: The register
heading: Escalate
text: A steward or leader can escalate a risk to a unit above its own, with a reason. The risk stays where it is and keeps its owner; escalation says "this needs you" to the leader above, and puts it among the risks at that level.

title: The register
heading: Close
text: Close a risk when it no longer applies, with the reason. It leaves the open register and stays findable, with its whole history.

title: The register
heading: The objectives it threatens
text: Risks → Objectives holds the organization's strategic objectives: what it means to achieve, over what period, and how it will know. A unit's leaders, or a manager, add them; the President's strategic plan is the usual source. A risk names the objectives it threatens, under Objectives it threatens on the risk (those who keep the risk). Each objective then lists exactly the risks that name it, with how each stands, and the list of objectives shows how many open risks threaten each, by rating. That is the register read against the strategic plan: which aims are most at risk, and from what. The register can be cut to the risks that threaten one objective. A risk's history keeps each objective it

title: The register
heading: The bow-tie
text: A risk's Bow-tie tab draws it left to right: what could cause the event, the controls that keep it from happening, the event, the controls that soften what follows, and the consequences. Nothing is entered for it. It reads the risk's own cause, event, and consequence, and the controls on its Controls tab: a control that reduces likelihood stands before the event, one that reduces impact after it, and one that reduces both on both sides, each with where it stands. A cause or consequence written one to a line, or with semicolons between, is drawn as several. A table below says the same for those who do not read diagrams.

title: The register
heading: Estimates in ranges
text: A rating on the program's scales is what the register is run by. For the risks worth putting a figure on, the risk's In numbers tab takes an estimate as ranges: how often a year (the fewest, the likely, and the most, where 0.1 is once in ten years) and what each time costs (the least, the likely, and the most), with what the numbers assume, which is required. An estimate is never edited: estimating anew supersedes the last, and every one is kept and in the history. A simulation then plays out ten thousand years: in each, the year's rate is drawn from a PERT distribution over the frequency range, the number of events from a Poisson distribution at that rate, and each event's cost from a PERT

title: The register
heading: Scenarios
text: Risks → Scenarios holds stories told on purpose: what might happen ("ransomware takes research computing down for two weeks"), what is assumed, the risks it would bring about or make worse and the processes it would stop, and, once it has been worked through, what was concluded. A scenario is kept by the stewards and leaders of its unit, and by assessors and managers, who work through scenarios with them; concluding one needs its conclusion. Where the risks it touches have estimates in ranges, the scenario shows what a simulation of them together comes to, taking them as independent, and names the risks it touches that have no estimate.

title: The register
heading: Controls
text: A control is something the organization does to make a risk less likely or less harmful. It has a statement of what is done, an owner, a unit, a kind (preventive, detective, corrective, or directive), and how often it happens. Controls → Library is your organization's own controls. Add a control can start from a set of 75 common controls in plain words: search it, choose one, and then make it specific. The starting text says "backups are tested"; yours says which systems, how often, and by whom.

title: The register
heading: Rate a control
text: What is known about a control is recorded as a rating with two parts and a note: Design: if it were done as described, would it work? Operation: is it actually done? Each is effective, partly effective, or ineffective. The note says what was looked at. As with assessments, a rating is never edited, only superseded. A control that has never been rated is not assessed , and a rating older than twelve months is out of date . Neither counts for anything until someone looks. A rating by its owner or a steward is a judgment. A rating from a test in an assessment, recorded by someone who does not own the control and confirmed by a second person, outranks it: while a test result holds, the control c

title: The register
heading: Link a control to a risk
text: On the risk's Controls tab, link each control that bears on it and say how: what it reduces : likelihood, impact, or both; how much the risk leans on it: primary (the risk relies on it) or supporting (it helps). A risk started from the library offers the controls commonly used for it.

title: The register
heading: What the controls suggest
text: Once a risk has an inherent rating and linked controls, RiskWren shows the residual rating the controls suggest, with its working: Each control counts by how well it is known to work: effective counts in full, partly effective counts half, and ineffective, not assessed, and out of date count nothing. A primary control counts in full; a supporting one counts half. The counts are added up for likelihood and for impact. Each whole point takes that axis down one level, by at most two levels. So a critical risk at likelihood 4 and impact 5, with one primary control that works, one that partly works, and impact controls adding up to one, is suggested at likelihood 3 and impact 4: high. The suggest

title: The register
heading: When the picture changes
text: If a control is later rated worse, or unlinked, and what the controls now suggest is worse than both the residual rating on record and what was suggested when it was made, the risk is flagged: its rating is in doubt , with the reason named. RiskWren never changes a rating by itself. It asks the owner to assess again.

title: The register
heading: Treatment
text: A risk above appetite needs an answer. On the risk's Treatment tab, record the response , with the reason: reduce it, accept it, transfer it (by contract or insurance), or avoid it (by stopping the activity).

title: The register
heading: Plans and actions
text: A treatment plan says what will be achieved, who owns it, by when, and the rating it aims for. Its actions are the steps, each with an owner and a due date. While a plan is active and its date has not passed, the risk is being treated . An action's owner marks it in progress and done. Moving its date needs a reason, and the original date and every move stay on the record. When a plan's last action is done, the plan is complete. That does not lower the rating: the risk is flagged, and its owner is asked for a new residual assessment that reflects what was actually achieved. A plan that passes its date with work still open no longer counts, and the risk needs a decision again. Treatment plans

title: The register
heading: Accept a risk
text: Accepting a risk is a decision by a named leader to live with what remains, for a stated reason, until a date. Three rules always hold: Nobody accepts a risk they own. It goes to a leader above. Only a leader of the risk's unit, or of a unit above it, may accept it, and for a high or critical risk only one whose limit reaches that rating. An acceptance expires. By default a moderate risk can be accepted for up to 24 months, a high one for 12, and a critical one for 6. If you may not accept a risk, its page says why and what is needed. An acceptance can carry conditions , the things that must stay true while it runs. An acceptance covers the rating that was accepted. If the residual rating la

title: The register
heading: Risk analyses
text: A risk analysis is a structured look at what is in a scope: each thing taken against each of a list of threats. It is the exercise a security rule or a funder asks for by name, and it leaves a report of what was considered. Risks → Analyses → Start a risk analysis (a steward, a manager, or an assessor). What to look at: what a scope 's boundary names, including everything held by the units it names; or everything a unit and the units beneath it hold. Only what is in use, and only what you may see. Which threats: whole categories of the risk library. Each library risk is one threat. One question is made for each thing against each threat, on the day it starts; the form says how many before yo

title: The register
heading: Find anything
text: Press ⌘K (or Ctrl K), or use the box at the top of every page, and type a name, a reference, or a few words. Records that match appear under the pages and actions; Search everything opens the full results. The search looks at every kind of record, and actions: in the name, the reference, the summary, and what a record is called in another system. Every word you type has to be on the record, in any order. Part of a word is enough. Results are grouped by kind, the closest match first. A reference typed exactly is its own best answer. You find only what you may open. A record you could not see on its own list is not in a search either, and is not counted.

title: The register
heading: Saved views
text: Every list keeps its filters and sort in the address, so a list as you have it can be kept. Views , beside the search box of each list, saves what is showing under a name and lists the views of that list. A view keeps the question and never the answer. Whoever opens it sees what they may see, as it stands that day. A view is yours alone unless it is shared. A steward, an assessor, a manager, an auditor, or an administrator can share one, which puts it on that list for everyone. Only whoever saved a view can rename or delete it. An administrator can take a shared one down.

title: The register
heading: What a record is missing
text: Each kind of record is expected to say a few things, and a record that does not yet says so under its title, with why it matters. Kind Expected Every kind below An owner who can sign in Processes, systems, third parties, information, services The class of data it handles; a link to anything else Third parties A tier Systems Where it is hosted Information Where it is held Risks A rating; a control that bears on it Controls A rating of how well it works Indicators A reading; a risk it warns of; where it is read from Only records still in use are counted: a retired system or a closed risk is not expected to be complete. A summary is not on the list, because many records are plain from their nam

title: The register
heading: The same thing written down twice
text: As you type the name of a new process, system, third party, information asset, risk, control, or issue, records already here that it might be are shown under the box. Open one in a new tab before adding another. Reports → Tidy also lists pairs that look like one thing: names with the same words in any order, or nearly the same spelling. Two units often keep a record each of the same thing on purpose, so across units only the very same name counts. Nothing is merged for you. Open both, keep the better one, move what the other holds, and retire it. If they are different things, someone who can edit either says so, and the pair is not suggested again.

title: The register
heading: Indicators
text: An indicator is a number someone already reads, kept where the risks it warns of can see it: servers patched within 30 days, days to remove a leaver's access, people who entered a password in the phishing exercise. Risks → Indicators → Add an indicator (a steward or a manager). Which way is worse , a warning level , and a limit . Patching is worse as it falls; open vulnerabilities are worse as they rise. The warning level is optional and must be reached before the limit. How often it is read: weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annually. Read from says where the number comes from, so whoever reads it next reads the same thing. The risks it warns of. Any open risk you may see. RiskWren does not fe

title: The register
heading: Seeing the whole
text: Register lists risks, with filters for category, residual rating, standing, and unit, a switch for the ones you are named on, and grouping by category or unit. Indicators lists every indicator with where it stands, and can show only those past their limit, past their warning level, or never read. Analyses lists the risk analyses, open and closed, each with how much of it has been answered. Heat map places every rated risk on the matrix, for the residual, inherent, or target rating, for a unit and everything beneath it, or for one category. Each cell opens the risks in it. Reports → Risk shows where the register stands, and Reports → Compliance how ready each scope is against what it is held

title: Compliance
heading: Compliance
text: Compliance This guide is for the people who answer for what the organization is held to: a security or compliance lead, the stewards of the units that must comply, and whoever reads the result. It covers frameworks, mapping controls to requirements, scopes, inherited controls, readiness, and the compliance dashboard. The idea is test once, satisfy many . A control is described once. It is mapped to every requirement it helps to meet, in as many frameworks as apply. It is tested once. What that test finds shows against every one of those requirements, in every scope that relies on the control.

title: Compliance
heading: Frameworks
text: A framework is any source of requirements: a federal rule, a security standard, the terms of a data use agreement, an internal standard. Compliance → Frameworks lists the ones on record. A new installation has four, each built from its publisher's own machine-readable file and carried as published: Framework What it is NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 Six functions, their categories, and 106 outcomes NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 The full control catalog, with the Low, Moderate, High, and Privacy baselines NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 The requirements for protecting controlled unclassified information HIPAA Security Rule 45 CFR Part 164 Subpart C, with its standards and implementation specifications Three

title: Compliance
heading: A framework of your own
text: An agreement's terms, a sponsor's security requirements, or an internal standard is entered as a framework and then behaves like any other. Frameworks → Add a framework (a manager for the whole organization, or an administrator). Give it a title and say what kind it is, then add its requirements: one at a time, with a code, a title, and the text; by Paste , a line each: a code, a space, then what it requires; by Import , from a spreadsheet saved as CSV with a code, a title, the text, and the code of the requirement each sits under. Paste and Import check everything first and add nothing unless every line can be added. A published framework is never edited; one of your own always can be, and

title: Compliance
heading: A new version of a framework
text: Frameworks change: a publisher revises a standard, a sponsor renews its terms. A new version is loaded beside the old one , never over it, and says which version it follows. Nothing that uses the old version changes when the new one arrives: its scopes, decisions, crosswalks, and exceptions stay exactly as they were until someone moves them. Compliance → Frameworks → Load a framework (a manager or an administrator) loads one that ships with RiskWren but is not loaded at first, such as SP 800-53 Rev. 4 for programs and agreements that still name it, or a pack from a file: a publisher's new version before RiskWren ships it, or a framework the organization keeps as a pack. Start a new version ,

title: Compliance
heading: Moving a scope to the new version
text: Move to (those who keep the scope) holds the scope to the new version in place of the old, starting from the baseline of the same name. What has the same code goes with it: its decisions about which requirements apply, with their reasons; the exceptions to those requirements within the scope; for the whole organization, the crosswalks and the documents mapped to the old version, to the same code, or to where the publisher says a withdrawn one went. A crosswalk carried to a different code answers in part, and says where it came from. A decision about a requirement the new version withdrew is left behind, and the scope's history says so, as it says each decision carried. The old version stays

title: Compliance
heading: Map controls to requirements
text: A mapping says that a control helps to satisfy a requirement, in full or in part , with a note if it needs one. From a control, open its Requirements tab: it lists what the control answers, in every framework, and adds more. From a requirement, open it in its framework: it lists the controls that answer it, and adds one. It also lists the published documents that answer it ( Policies ). A control started from the library of common controls arrives already mapped: 46 of the 75 carry suggested mappings to the built-in frameworks. The other 29 are about things no security framework asks for, such as cold storage, research integrity, and finance. Between them the 46 answer 80 of the Cybersecurit

title: Compliance
heading: Crosswalks a publisher's mapping suggests
text: Some publishers say how their framework relates to another. SP 800-171 Rev. 3 names the SP 800-53 controls each of its requirements comes from, and RiskWren carries that with the pack. From it, a control mapped to one side is suggested for the requirement on the other: a control mapped to SP 800-171's 03.01.01 is suggested for AC-2 and the enhancements it was derived from, and the other way around. A framework with suggestions waiting says so on its page. Review them lists them control by control, each with what suggests it. Map it maps the control, in part, and it is yours like any crosswalk. Not this one sets the suggestion aside, and it is not suggested again. Nothing is mapped until a pe

title: Compliance
heading: Scopes
text: A scope is a boundary that must meet one or more frameworks: the clinical systems, a data enclave, central computing, the whole organization. Compliance → Scopes → Add a scope (a steward of the unit, or a manager). A scope says four things. What is inside it. On Overview → Inside the boundary , list the units, processes, systems, information assets, and third parties it covers. What it is held to. Held to → Add a framework. Start from every requirement, or from a baseline where the framework has them. Which requirements apply. On the Requirements tab, every requirement applies until someone says otherwise. Leave out takes one out, and needs a reason; Bring back returns it. Only the departure

title: Compliance
heading: Inherited controls
text: A central team runs backup, identity, and the network once, for everyone. A scope that provides controls says so: edit it and tick Offers its controls to other scopes . Another scope then uses Controls → Inherit a control , and chooses how: How What it means Inherited The provider does all of it. The control stands in this scope exactly where it stands in theirs, and slips the day theirs does Shared The provider does part and this scope does the rest. It says what its part is and where that stands, and the control is as far along as the weaker half People in the inheriting scope see whose control they rely on, where it stands, and how well it is known to work, without being able to open the

title: Compliance
heading: Agreements
text: Compliance → Agreements holds what the organization has promised others: an award's terms, a data use agreement, a business associate agreement, a contract, a confidentiality agreement, a memorandum of understanding. Add an agreement (a steward or leader of the unit that answers for it, or a manager) records: who it is with , and their reference for it; when it runs : the day it starts and the day it ends, or none for one that runs until it is ended; its notice period : how many days before it ends notice must be given, to end it or to keep it going, and whether it carries on by itself unless notice is given; its terms : the framework of the requirements it imposes. That is usually its own t

title: Compliance
heading: What it covers, and what that binds
text: Who it is with names the third parties it binds, from the inventory, beside the words of With . What it covers names the systems, the bodies of information, the services, and the scopes the agreement binds; together they say whether the information a third party holds is covered, as Coverage describes. Then every scope that is one of them, or holds one of them inside its boundary, is held to the agreement's terms , without anyone adding the framework by hand. On the scope's page the framework says why: because AGR-0003 covers what it holds . Its requirements are answered like any others, and the agreement's page lists the scopes it binds. The scopes follow the agreement as it changes. Cover

title: Compliance
heading: Dates and warnings
text: An agreement is in force , ending (within 60 days of its end), notice due (within 30 days of the last day to give notice), ended but still open, or closed . Its owners are told, under the bell and by email where it is set up, and it is on their Home: When What 30 days before the last day to give notice Give notice, or let it carry on 60 days before it ends Renew it, or let it end After it has ended, while it is still open The same people, then the unit's steward after 7 days and its leader after 21 An agreement that has ended stays open, and what it imposes still binds its scopes, until someone records its new end date ( Edit ) or closes it with the reason. That way nothing it imposed drops

title: Compliance
heading: Readiness
text: For a scope and a framework, each requirement that applies is in exactly one state. It is worked out and never typed in. State Rule Verified Every control that answers it here is in place, has been tested and found effective, and has evidence that still counts In place Every control that answers it here is said to be in place, and at least one lacks a test that still holds or current evidence Excepted It would be planned, a gap, or failing, and an approved exception that covers it is in force today Planned A control that answers it is used here and is not yet in place Gap No control mapped to it is used in this scope Failing A test that still holds found a control that answers it partly effe

title: Compliance
heading: The security plan and OSCAL
text: A scope's Requirements tab has two more downloads beside Print and the export: Security plan is the scope's system security plan, in the customary order: system identification (name, reference, unit, owners), the description and authorization boundary, what the system includes, the frameworks it is held to, then for each framework every requirement in the catalog's order with where it stands and, for each control that answers it, the implementation statement here (or the provider's, for an inherited control), its responsibility, and where it stands; requirements left out with their reason; and last, the plan of action. It is a page that prints by itself, opened from the download. OSCAL is th
