title: Compliance
heading: Connections
text: Every record has a Connections link beside its name. It opens a picture of what the record is joined to: what it relies on and what relies on it, the risks that bear on it, the controls that reduce them, the documents that direct those controls, the scopes it sits in, and the evidence, issues, exceptions, and assessments about it. The button on a neighbor shows what lies beyond it without leaving the page, and choosing a neighbor puts it in the middle. A list beside the picture says the same in full, so nothing is told by the picture alone. Everything in it can be reached and opened with the keyboard. For a security lead this answers the questions that come up in an incident or a review: wha

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Evidence and testing
text: Evidence and testing This guide is for the people who collect proof that a control is done, and for those who test whether it works: control owners, assessors, and whoever leads an assessment. It covers evidence, its dates, files, assessments, tests, independence, and what a result changes.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Evidence
text: An evidence item is something that shows a control is done. It is collected once and attached to everything it supports. Kind What it is A file A report, an export, a screenshot, a signed form A link Where the proof lives in another system A note of what was seen What somebody looked at, and what they saw An attestation A named person's statement that something is so Compliance → Evidence → Add evidence , or Add evidence on a control or a scope, which attaches it there as it is made. Anyone may add evidence for a unit they work in, because the people who do the work hold the proof. Every item has an owner, the date it was collected, the period it covers, a data class, and the date it holds u

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Evidence stops counting
text: Evidence is true of a moment. An item holds for twelve months from the day it was collected unless you give another date, and it is in one of three states: State Meaning Current It counts Expires soon It counts, and its date is within 30 days. Its owner sees it on Home No longer counts Its date has passed. It stays on the record, and counts toward nothing Stale evidence is never deleted and never quietly renewed. Collect it again and add a new item; the old one remains as what was true then.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Attach it
text: An item counts once it is attached to the control it shows. On the item, Supports → Edit lists the controls and scopes it is attached to. One item can support many: the same restore log may be evidence for a backup control and for the scope that relies on it. Putting evidence on a control or a scope is for those who keep or assess that control or scope. Collecting is open; attaching is not.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Files
text: A file is checked by what it contains, not by its name. PDF, common images, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint documents, and plain text (including CSV and JSON) are taken, up to 25 MB. Programs are refused. Files are stored under the SHA-256 of their content, in the data home, in a directory the server does not serve from. The same file sent twice is kept once. A file only ever leaves as a download. A page or a drawing kept as evidence of a configuration is stored and returned as the plain text it is, so it cannot run in the browser. Every download is recorded in the item's history.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Who sees evidence
text: Evidence is more closely held than the register. An item is seen by whoever collected it, those named on it, and those with a role over its unit. Others see it only through something it is attached to that they may see, and not at all if it is restricted or of the most sensitive data class. A person who cannot see a control cannot download its evidence.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Assessments
text: An assessment is a planned look at whether a scope's controls work. Compliance → Assessments → Start an assessment (an assessor or a manager), or Start an assessment on a scope. Give it a name, the scope, a period, and a lead. It plans a test for each control the scope does itself: every one of them; or with Against set to a framework, only those that answer a requirement of it that applies in the scope. A control the scope inherits is not tested here. It is tested where it is provided, once, and the result reaches every scope that relies on it.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Plan the tests
text: Each test has a method (examine records and settings, interview the people who do it, or test it and see), a procedure , and a person it is assigned to . Plan on a test changes them. A test that is assigned appears on that person's Home, due on the last day of the assessment's period.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Record a result
text: Record result on a test: Design : would it reduce the risk, if it operated as described? Operation : does it operate as described? What was looked at : the sample, the period, the people asked. What was found. This is required. Evidence : cite the items that show it. Each of design and operation is effective, partly effective, or ineffective. The control is as strong as the weaker of the two.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Independence, and a second pair of eyes
text: Two rules always hold, and the server enforces both. Nobody records or reviews a result for a control they own. The test is shown to them as theirs, with someone else to do it. A result counts only when a second person has confirmed it. Whoever recorded it cannot confirm it. Recording a result changes nothing. It waits, and the assessment's lead sees it on Home. Review then either confirms it or returns it with a note saying what needs another look. A returned result is recorded again; the earlier one stays in the assessment's history.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: What a confirmed result changes
text: Confirming a result does three things at once. It becomes the control's rating , on the basis of a test, in the tester's name. It moves every requirement the control answers, in every scope that relies on it. Effective, with evidence that still counts, makes them verified. Partly effective or ineffective makes them failing, in the scope that does the control and in every scope that inherits it. It moves the residual rating that the controls suggest for every risk the control reduces. If the suggestion is now worse than the rating on record, the risk is flagged as in doubt and its owner is asked to assess again. A result of partly effective or ineffective also opens an issue for the control's

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Finish
text: Complete closes an assessment once every test in it has a result that counts. A test that will not be done is taken out first. Cancel it abandons an assessment; results already confirmed still count. The assessment's History tab tells every test planned, every result recorded, and every confirmation and return, with who did each.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: An attestation is not a test
text: A control's owner can be asked, in a campaign , whether it still operates as described. Their answer is recorded on the control and shown there, apart from its rating: who said it, when, and what they said. That is the owner's word. It is worth having, and it is a different kind of assurance from a test by someone who does not own the control. RiskWren keeps the two apart by rule: An attestation never makes anything verified. A control its owner says is working is in place, and the reason given says it rests on an attestation and no test. An attestation can take a control out of verified. If a test found a control effective and its owner has since said it operates only partly, or not at all,

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Verified, in practice
text: A requirement is verified when each control that answers it in the scope is in place, has a confirmed test result of effective that still holds, and has current evidence, either attached to the control or cited by that result. So the working rhythm for a control owner and an assessor is: The owner keeps the control's evidence current, renewing it before its date. The assessor tests the control once a year and cites that evidence. A second assessor confirms the result. Miss the first and the requirement drops to in place when the evidence goes stale. Miss the second and it drops when the test is a year old. Neither needs anyone to notice: the scope's Requirements tab and the compliance dashbo

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Issues and exceptions
text: Issues and exceptions This guide is for whoever has to put something right, whoever checks that it was, and whoever decides when a departure is allowed for a while. It covers the issue register, severity and dates, actions, closure, exceptions, the plan of action, and notices.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Issues
text: An issue is something found to be wrong that must be put right. Compliance → Issues is one register for all of them, whatever found them: Found by For example A test An assessment found a control partly effective or ineffective A gap A requirement that nothing answers in a scope Security testing A penetration test, a scan, or an exercise An audit A finding from an internal or external audit An incident Something that went wrong showed it A review A review of a supplier, a system, or a process An observation Somebody noticed it and said so

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Raise an issue
text: Issues → Raise an issue. Anyone may raise one for a unit they work in or have a role over. Say what is wrong, in which unit, how serious it is, what found it, and what it is about: the controls, scopes, and risks concerned. Name who is to put it right; they are told. On a scope's Requirements tab, Raise an issue beside a requirement that is a gap, planned, or failing starts one already about that requirement and that scope.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: From a failed test
text: When a test result of partly effective or ineffective is confirmed, an issue is opened without anyone asking: it is named for the control and the assessment, and carries what the test found and what was looked at; it is high if the control was found ineffective and moderate if partly effective; it belongs to the control's owners, who are told, and not to whoever found it; it names every scope that relies on the control. If an issue is already open for that control from an earlier test, that one stands and no second one is opened. If the control has no owner the issue has none either, and shows on Home for those who can name one.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Severity sets the date
text: Each severity has a written meaning, shown as you choose, and the issue is due a fixed time after it was raised: Severity Due within Critical 30 days High 90 days Moderate 180 days Low 365 days The table is part of the program and can be changed (see Running the program ). Changing an issue's severity applies the rule again, counted from the day it was raised. Move the date changes it by hand. That needs a reason, and where the date started and every move stay on the record, with a count beside the date wherever the issue is listed.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Put it right
text: An issue is worked through actions , each with an owner and a date: the same actions treatment plans use, on the same list of everything owed. Add an action on the issue. Whoever owns an action sees the issue, does their part, and marks it done.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Close it
text: Its owner chooses Propose closure , and says what was done, why it happened (a root cause from a short list: procedure, people and time, ownership, technology, design, change, third party, or other), and cites the evidence that shows it. Open actions must be finished or cancelled first. The issue then waits. An assessor or a manager for the unit sees it on Home and chooses Confirm closure : either confirming, which closes it, or sending it back with a note saying what is still missing. Nobody confirms the closure of an issue they own, or one they proposed closing. The server refuses it. Two more things belong to the second line alone: Withdraw , for an issue raised in error, and Reopen , for

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Who sees an issue
text: An issue is known to those with a part in it: whoever raised it, those named on it, anyone with an action on it, and those with a role over its unit. Working in the unit is not enough. An issue can also be marked restricted.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Exceptions
text: An exception is an approved departure from a control, a requirement, or a document, for a time, with what makes up for it. It is the honest answer when something cannot be met yet and everyone knows it.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Ask
text: An exception is asked for from a scope, by those who keep it: on the Requirements tab, Ask for an exception beside a requirement that is a gap, planned, or failing; on the Controls tab, Exception beside a control, including one the scope inherits and cannot fix itself. An exception to a policy, standard, or procedure is asked for from the document's own page, and decided by a leader or manager of the unit that keeps it ( Policies ). Say why it is needed, what is done in its place meanwhile, and the dates it runs between. It is never open-ended: by default it runs for at most twelve months.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Decide
text: A leader or a manager with authority over the unit decides, and whoever asked does not decide . They see the request on Home. Approving may shorten it; refusing needs a reason. Asking changes nothing: an exception covers nothing until it is approved.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: While it is in force, and after
text: While an exception is in force, what it covers is shown as excepted in place of failing, a gap, or planned, with the state underneath said beside it. It does not improve on a control that is in place. The day after it ends, the state underneath is back, without anyone doing anything. Nothing has to run for that to happen: whether an exception is in force is worked out from its dates on the day. Whoever asked sees it on Home a month before it ends. Ask again starts a new request that carries on from it, which is decided again. End it early withdraws one that is no longer needed. Compliance → Exceptions lists them, and can show those waiting to be decided, in force, ended, refused, or withdraw

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Findings of internal audit
text: An issue raised by internal audit from an engagement says so on its page. Its closure is confirmed by an auditor rather than by an assessor or a manager, and only auditors withdraw or reopen it. See Findings and follow-up .

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: The plan of action
text: A scope's Plan of action tab lists the open issues that bear on it: those about the scope itself, and those about any control it uses or inherits. They are listed most severe first, each with its owner, its milestones (the actions, with who and when), and its date. It prints, and it is the document a reviewer asks for: what is wrong, who is fixing it, and by when. OSCAL downloads it as a plan of action and milestones in the open assessment language; see The security plan and OSCAL .

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Notices
text: The bell at the top right counts what has been assigned to you or decided for you since you last looked: an issue handed to you, an action that is yours, a closure sent back, an exception approved or refused, a request waiting for your decision. A notice is a sentence and a place to go. It is not the record of what happened, which is in the history, and nobody is told about what they did themselves. Home remains the list of what you still owe.

title: Policies
heading: Policies
text: Policies This guide is for whoever writes, approves, or keeps the organization's policies, standards, procedures, and guidelines: most often the security office and the compliance office, and the leaders who approve what they write. RiskWren holds each document with its versions, who approved each one, and when it is next looked at. The words can be written here, or stay where the organization already keeps them; either way the lifecycle is tracked here. Everyone reads what applies to them in the policy library , and says they have where a document asks them to.

title: Policies
heading: Documents
text: Policies → Documents lists them all, broadest first. It is in the menu of stewards, leaders, assessors, managers, and those who read everything; anyone named an owner of a document reaches it from the document in the library. A document is one of five kinds: Kind What it is Policy What the organization requires, and why. Approved by its leadership. Standard The particular rules that meet a policy: how long a password, which encryption. Procedure The steps someone follows to meet a standard or a policy. Continuity plan What to do to keep a process going, or to bring it back, when something stops it. Written, approved, and reviewed like any document; what it restores, its exercises, and a copy

title: Policies
heading: Writing a version
text: A document's words are in its versions. The Next version tab is where the next one is written, in one of three ways: Write it here , in a simple Markdown: # for a heading, - for a list, **bold** , *emphasis* , [a link](https://…) , and tables. Preview shows it as it will read. A document of three or more sections gets a list of contents. Link to where it is kept , such as a page on the intranet or a file in the document library. RiskWren keeps its approvals, its dates, and its address. Attach a file : a PDF or a Word document, up to 25 MB. A new version starts as a copy of the one in force. What changed, and why is needed before a second or later version is sent; it is shown with the version

title: Policies
heading: Approval
text: Send it for approval names the people who must approve it. Each is told, and it appears on their Home. Nobody approves their own work. The person who sends a version, and the person who started it, cannot be among those who approve it. Each approves it, or returns it with a reason. A return sends it back to its author with the reason on the draft; those still to decide are no longer asked. When the author sends it again, everyone named is asked again. What is under review is not changed. To change it, take it back . Those not yet asked are told they no longer need to approve it. When everyone has approved it, its owners are told and it can be published.

title: Policies
heading: Publishing
text: Publish puts the approved version in force. It is numbered (version 1, 2, 3), the version before it is superseded, and its next review is set from that day. A published version is never changed. No screen or route edits it; a correction is a new version. The history keeps each version's fingerprint , taken when it was published, and riskwren verify checks every published version against it: text altered in the database, or a file changed in the data home, is reported. Versions lists every published version with who approved it and what changed. Any two can be compared side by side: lines added, removed, or reworded, with the words that differ marked. A step put in the middle of a list shows

title: Policies
heading: Review
text: Each document is looked at again on a cadence: every 12 months as shipped, or its own if it sets one under Reviewed every . The program's cadence is changed under Admin → Program → Cadences, which moves the next review of every document that follows it. When a review comes due it shows on the document, on its owners' Home, and in the reminders: before its date, when it passes, then to the unit's steward and its leader. Look at it, then either: Review and keep , saying what was looked at. The version stays in force and the next review moves on; the review is in the history. Start a new version , and send it for approval as above. Publishing it sets the next review. A document no longer needed

title: Policies
heading: What it governs
text: A document is connected to what it governs on its What it governs tab, by those who may change it: The controls it directs. A control a document directs is how what the document requires is done: the access control standard directs account approval, access reviews, and removing access on leaving. Add a control finds one by name or reference. The requirements it answers. A requirement a document answers is one the organization meets, at least in part, by saying so in it: the information security policy answers the Cybersecurity Framework's GV.PO-01 and the HIPAA Security Rule's 164.316(a). Add a requirement chooses a framework and finds the requirement by code or words. Each side shows the ot

title: Policies
heading: Exceptions to a document
text: A unit that cannot follow a document for a time asks for an exception to it, as it would to a control or a requirement ( Issues and exceptions ): Ask for an exception on the document's page, saying why, what it does instead, and until when. Who asks: a unit's steward, leader, or manager, or those who keep the document. A member of staff asks their steward. Who decides: a leader or a manager of the unit that keeps the document, and never whoever asked. A departure from the security office's encryption standard is decided by the security leader, whichever lab asks. It ends by its dates, like every exception. While it is in force the document's page lists it, and the day after it ends it is sho

title: Policies
heading: Who it applies to
text: A document applies to everyone , as shipped, or to the people chosen under Who it applies to on its page: those who work in chosen units , and in the units beneath them, and those who hold chosen roles , wherever they hold them: every steward, say, or every manager. Someone in a chosen unit or holding a chosen role is one person, counted once. An account that is disabled is no longer counted. Who it applies to decides what each person finds in their library and who is asked to acknowledge it; it does not decide who may read it, which follows the document's unit and restriction like any record.

title: Policies
heading: The policy library
text: Policies → Policy library is where everyone reads the documents in force: the published version of each document that applies to them, broadest first, with what they still have to acknowledge at the top. Everything published shows every document they may read, whether or not it applies to them. The search finds a word in a title, a summary, or the text. A document opens to read as it is in force: its version, when it came into force, who approved it, what changed in it, and the documents above and beneath it. Drafts, approvals, and earlier versions are not shown here; they are on the document's own page, under Policies → Documents , which those who write and keep documents use. The library i

title: Policies
heading: Acknowledgment
text: A document can ask the people it applies to to say they have read it: tick Ask those it applies to to say they have read it when adding or editing it. Then: Each version that is published asks again. Those it applies to are told, and it stays on their Home until they have. At the end of the document they press I have read it and understand it . What they acknowledged, and when, is kept with the version. A change that does not alter what anyone must do need not ask again. Untick Everyone must acknowledge this version again on the next version, for a correction or a broken link: what people said of the version before still counts. Every version asks again unless its author says otherwise. An a

title: Policies
heading: Who has acknowledged it
text: The document's Acknowledgments tab shows everyone it applies to, split by whether they have acknowledged the version they must: as a count, by unit with the units that have most still to do first, and person by person. Someone who acknowledged an earlier version that no longer counts is shown with it. The tab is for the document's owners and editors, assessors of its unit, and those who read everything.

title: Policies
heading: Asking for it by a date
text: Ask for acknowledgment on that tab (an assessor or a manager) starts an acknowledgment campaign : those it applies to, or only those in one unit and beneath it, are asked by a date. Those who have already acknowledged the version they must are counted as answered from the start. Everyone else finds it on their Home with the date, is reminded as it approaches, and answers by acknowledging it in the library; the campaign's page shows coverage by unit as they do. The same campaign can be started from Compliance → Campaigns ( Running the program ).

title: Third parties
heading: Third parties
text: Third parties This guide is for whoever looks after the organization's suppliers, service providers, and partners: most often the security office, which asks how each handles the organization's information, and the units that rely on each. A third party has been a record of the inventory from the start: a name, a unit, owners, and links to the processes it performs and the systems it supplies. This guide is about what RiskWren adds to that: what each third party provides, how much is at stake with it, what it says about itself when asked, what independent reports say about it, whether an agreement covers what is shared with it, and how the relationship goes on and ends.

title: Third parties
heading: Third parties and their services
text: Third parties → Third parties lists every supplier, service provider, contractor, collaborator, sponsor, and subrecipient, with its tier. Third parties → Services lists what they provide. A service ( SVC-0001 ) is what the organization gets from a third party: the hosted clinical record system, the maintenance contract for the freezer farm, the tests the clinical laboratory sends out. It is a record of the inventory beside its third party, with its own unit, criticality, data class, and owners. A third party with three services may hold restricted information through one and nothing through the others, so it is the services that say what a third party touches: From Link To Service reaches Sy

title: Third parties
heading: Tiering
text: A third party's tier says how much is at stake with it, and so how closely it is reviewed. The program has four, as shipped: Tier What puts a third party in it Reviewed Tier 1 It holds or can see restricted or regulated information, has privileged access to systems, or is relied on for critical work and reaches information or systems Every 12 months Tier 2 It holds confidential information, reaches the network, accounts, or systems, holds records about 500 or more people, or critical work stops without it Every 24 months Tier 3 It holds internal information, works on the premises, passes work on to others, holds information outside the United States, or would be missed Every 36 months Tier 4

title: Third parties
heading: Due diligence
text: A review ( DDR-0001 ) asks a third party about itself: a questionnaire, sent to one of its contacts through a link, answered without an account, and read by someone here who records what they concluded. Third parties → Due diligence lists them all, and each third party's Due diligence tab lists its own, with its contacts.

title: Third parties
heading: Contacts
text: A contact is a person at the third party who can be asked: a name, an email address, and their role there. Contacts are not accounts and never sign in. Those who keep the third party, and assessors, add them on its Due diligence tab, and say when one has left; the tab, and their addresses, are shown to those people and to those who read everything.

title: Third parties
heading: Start a review
text: Start a review on the third party's Due diligence tab. The questionnaire is the one its tier names, as shipped: Tier Questionnaire Tier 1 Due diligence: full , about forty-five questions: governance, access, the organization's information, health information, building and changing the service, operations, incidents, continuity, and the others it uses Tier 2 Due diligence: standard , about twenty-five questions on the same ground Tier 3 Due diligence: short , eight questions Tier 4 None: choose one if a review is wanted at all The questionnaires are written for organizations in the United States: they ask about a business associate agreement where health information is involved, about notice

title: Third parties
heading: Send it
text: Send it chooses the contact, the date the answers are wanted by (three weeks on, unless another is given), and how long the link lasts (30 days unless said, at most 90). The link is shown once, to copy, and is sent to the contact by email where email is set up. The link is the contact's way in, and nothing else is: It is a long random token. Only a digest of it is kept, so nobody can read it back from the database, and a message that carried it is cleared once it has been sent. The token follows a # in the address. Browsers never send that part to a server, so it is not in any server's or proxy's logs. It opens one thing: the questionnaire of that review, as that contact. It reaches no other

title: Third parties
heading: Review the answers
text: When the answers come in, the review's owners are told, and it waits on their Home. The review shows the answers as they were asked. Some answers are marked by the questionnaire as concerns : no second factor, critical updates applied only after a month or more, an incident reported in the last three years, information held outside the United States, no independent report. They are listed first, with how many of the answers the questionnaire marks are concerns. They are what to look at, and decide nothing. Conclude records what was concluded: approved , approved with conditions , or not approved . Conditions, and a refusal, say what must change, or why. A review whose answers are late, or wh

title: Third parties
heading: Assurance documents
text: A report or certificate is what someone independent found: a SOC 2 Type II report, an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate, a HITRUST certification, a penetration test summary, a bridge letter. Each is held as an item of evidence on the third party, with the period it covers and the date it holds until. Past that date it no longer counts, and its owners are told beforehand, as with any evidence. Reports are confidential: they are seen by their owners, the third party's unit's stewards, leaders, and managers, assessors, and those who read everything, and not by everyone who can see the third party. The third party's Assurance tab lists them, newest first, each with whether it is in date and what its rev

title: Third parties
heading: Review a report
text: A report says less than its cover suggests until someone reads it. Review it records what a careful reader notes: What it is , who issued it, and the opinion : unqualified, qualified, adverse, or none (a certificate, or a test summary). The services it covers. Those not ticked are listed as services it does not cover, so a report on the identity service is not taken to vouch for the mail service added since. What is carved out : the parts left to others the third party uses, such as the data centres it runs in. Each exception the auditor noted , whether it matters here, and what is done about it. What it leaves to the organization. A SOC report lists complementary user entity controls: what

title: Third parties
heading: Coverage
text: Information is shared with a third party when it is linked as shared with it, or when one of its services handles it. The program says which kinds of agreement shared information needs. As shipped, written for the United States: When It needs Patient records are handled by a service provider, contractor, or supplier A business associate agreement, under HIPAA Participant data or patient records are shared with a collaborator, sponsor, or subrecipient A data use agreement, or the terms of the award or contract it is shared for Controlled-access data is shared with anyone A data use agreement Restricted information is shared with anyone A contract, a confidentiality agreement, a business assoc

title: Third parties
heading: Findings
text: A concern in a review's answers, or anything else a review turns up, is followed up as an issue. Raise a finding on the review (or Raise it as a finding beside one concern) raises an issue about the third party, found by review , which names the review it came from. Like any issue it has a severity, a date by its severity, owners here, and actions. An action on such an issue can be done by one of the third party's contacts: say who, when adding it. The contact has no account; the action's owner here follows it up with them, is reminded of its date, and records when it is done. The issue closes, as every issue does, when someone who does not own it confirms the fix.

title: Third parties
heading: Review again
text: Each third party is due for review on the cadence its tier sets (as shipped, every 12, 24, or 36 months, and Tier 4 only when called for), counted from its last concluded review, or from when it was first tiered if it has never been reviewed. Next review on its page says when, and why. A review due within a month, or late, is on Home for those who keep the third party and in the reminders; the list of third parties can be cut to those whose review is due. Something can call for a review sooner: an incident at the supplier, a breach notice, a change to what it does for the organization or to who owns it. Call for a review records what happened, and makes it due at once. Concluding the next re

title: Third parties
heading: Ending a relationship
text: End the relationship opens a checklist: Access removed : its accounts, remote access, and badges here. Information returned or destroyed , with a certificate where there is one. Agreements ended : closed, or noted for what survives them. Its attestation recorded : its written confirmation that nothing of the organization's is kept. Each step is recorded by someone who keeps the third party, saying what was done. When the last is recorded, the third party and its services are retired; until then it is shown as being offboarded. Offboarding can be stopped, and the history keeps every step.

title: Third parties
heading: Subcontractors
text: A third party names the third parties it depends on with a link, Subcontracts to , read from the other side as Is a subcontractor of . Both are in the Connections picture, so a supplier that several of the organization's suppliers rely on in turn is easy to see.

title: Internal audit
heading: Internal audit
text: Internal audit This guide is for internal audit, the third line: those who decide what is worth auditing, plan a period's work, and carry it out on the same record the first and second lines keep. Auditors read every record and its history, as before, and change none of them. What this guide covers is the audit function's own records: the universe, the plans, and the engagements in them.

title: Internal audit
heading: The universe
text: Audit → Universe lists everything worth auditing: every unit beneath the organization, and every process, system, third party, and scope in use. Nothing is kept by hand: a thing joins the universe when it is added to the inventory, and leaves when it is retired. Each is ranked by what the register says about it today, highest first. A ranking is the sum of its parts, and How beside it shows each part with the points it gave: Part Points Its worst open risk Up to 30, by where the residual rating of the worst open risk that concerns it sits on the scale. For a unit, the risks of the unit and everything beneath it Risks above appetite 4 for each open risk above appetite, up to 16 Open issues 2

title: Internal audit
heading: What audit says about a thing
text: An auditor's Say beside a thing records what audit knows that the register does not: Move it up or down, by up to 30 points either way, with the reason: a tip-off, a change of system, a regulator's interest. The move is a part of its ranking like any other, with the reason as its label. An audit before RiskWren: when it was last audited, and by whom, so that it is not counted as never audited. Leave it out, with the reason: a thing another body audits, or one too small to be worth it. Left out lists them. Everything audit says is in the history.

title: Internal audit
heading: The plan
text: Audit → Plans holds a plan for each period: the engagements internal audit means to carry out, each on one thing from the universe, with the reason for it and when it is planned. An auditor drafts a plan and plans its engagements, choosing from the universe, highest ranked first. A plan is approved by someone with the standing to: an auditor other than the one who drafted it, recording the approval of the audit committee (say on whose authority, and when), or a leader of the whole organization. A plan with nothing in it is not approved. Once approved it is tracked against: each engagement says where it stands (planned, under way, reported, or dropped), and the plan counts them. An engagement

title: Internal audit
heading: Engagements
text: An engagement planned in a plan is started by an auditor, with its lead, the rest of its team (auditors all), and what it covers. It then moves through its stages, each moved on by its lead: Stage Moves on when Planning The program of work has at least one step Fieldwork Every workpaper is signed off Reporting The report is written: what the engagement found, and an opinion (effective, needs improvement, or ineffective) Reported It is done. title: Internal audit
heading: Workpapers
text: Each step of the program of work has a workpaper : what was to be done, what was done, what was found, and the evidence, by reference to items of evidence already kept. Whoever records the work is its preparer . Another member of the team reviews it: a review note asks about something, the preparer answers it, and the one who wrote it clears it. A workpaper is signed off by a member of the team other than its preparer, once every note on it is cleared. Recording the work again after sign-off, or a new note, undoes the sign-off.

title: Internal audit
heading: Requests to the audited
text: While an engagement is being planned or in fieldwork, its team asks the audited for what it needs: Ask for something on the engagement, with what is needed, the person asked (anyone who can sign in), and by when. The request is on that person's home page. They see what is asked, by whom, for which engagement, and by when, and nothing else of the engagement's work. They answer in words, with evidence, or both. The evidence already kept about the thing being audited (and, for a scope, about the controls it uses) is offered first, so that nothing already on file is sent again; anything else is added under Compliance → Evidence first and named by its reference. The answer is on the team's home p

title: Internal audit
heading: Independence
text: Until an engagement is reported, its work is its team's alone. Others who may read the plans see that it exists, who is on it, and where it stands, and nothing of what it covers, what was done, or what was found; neither does another auditor who is not on its team. The history records every change to a workpaper, a review note, and a request, but keeps their words out of it, so that reading the history does not undo that. Once the report is issued, the whole of it opens to those who read the plans.

title: Internal audit
heading: Findings and follow-up
text: During fieldwork or reporting, the team raises a finding : what was found, its severity, and the manager who answers for putting it right. A finding is an issue in the one register everyone works from, marked as coming from internal audit and from which engagement; its date follows from its severity like any other. It is shared with management as soon as it is raised, which is how its action plan is agreed: management's action plan is the issue's actions, each with an owner and a date. See Issues and exceptions . When management says it is put right, it is internal audit, not the second line, that confirms it closed , or sends it back with what is missing: any auditor other than its owner an

title: Internal audit
heading: The committee report
text: Each plan's Committee report is the page for the audit committee: the plan and who approved it; each engagement with what it audits, where it stands, its opinion, and how many findings it raised and how many are still open; the findings by severity, open and closed; and the findings and management's actions past their date. It prints by itself.

heading: Running the program
text: Running the program This guide is for the risk, compliance, and security assurance team and for administrators. It covers roles and scope, who sees what, shaping the program, the dashboards, the history, and appearance.

title: Running the program
heading: Two kinds of authority
text: RiskWren keeps administration and judgment apart. An administrator manages accounts, units, appearance, and system settings. That role reads the register and can set the program's rules, since it sets everything else up. It does not assess, rate, or accept. A manager runs the program: shapes the categories, appetite, and scoring method, edits any record, and reads everything. A manager does not accept risk either. Acceptance belongs to leaders. Someone who does both jobs holds both roles, and the history shows which they acted under.

title: Running the program
heading: Roles and scope
text: Four roles can be limited to a unit, and then cover that unit and everything beneath it: manager, assessor, leader, and steward. title: Running the program
heading: Categories
text: Add a category at the top of the tree or beneath a category that is there. A category at the top needs an appetite of its own. Edit renames one, describes it, or retires it: a retired category is not offered to new risks, and risks already in it keep it. The arrows put categories in the order people will choose from.

title: Running the program
heading: Appetite
text: Appetite is the highest residual rating the organization will live with for a kind of risk without a plan or an acceptance. It is set for each top category and can be set differently for any category beneath; one that sets none takes its parent's. As shipped, clinical, regulatory, and financial risk have a low appetite, strategic risk a high one, and the rest moderate. Changing one is previewed first, because it changes which risks need a decision.

title: Running the program
heading: Scales and matrix

Every open risk is read again from the matrix now in force, so the register always speaks one language. title: Running the program
heading: Vocabularies
text: Choose a list, then rename its values, say what each means, put them in order, add one, or retire one. Records store a value's key, never its name , so renaming a value rewrites nothing. A new value's key is made from its name and never changes. A value in use is retired, not removed. Records that have it keep it; new records cannot choose it. Some lists can only be renamed. A severity sets a clock, a kind of link says what it joins, an owner kind decides who may edit. Their names, meanings, and order can be changed here; values are added or taken away with a program pack. A value new records start with cannot be retired , such as a system's lifecycle "in service".

title: Running the program
heading: Who may accept what
text: The table on the Program page shows, for each rating, how often a risk is reviewed and who may accept it when it is above appetite: Residual rating Reviewed every May be accepted Low 24 months No acceptance is needed Moderate 12 months For up to 24 months, by a leader of the unit or above High 6 months For up to 12 months, by a leader whose limit reaches high Critical 3 months For up to 6 months, by a leader whose limit reaches critical A leader's limit is set with the role. A sensible start: unit leaders at moderate, division leaders at high, and one or two executives at critical.

Admin → Questionnaires lists them. Anyone signed in can read one and try it; those who run the program change them. title: Running the program
heading: Questions that appear by condition
text: A question, or a whole section, can be asked only when an earlier answer makes it relevant. "What is different from the statement?" is asked only of someone who said the control operates partly or not at all. So nobody answers what does not apply to them, and what is asked is short. A rule looks only at questions asked before it, so showing and hiding can never run in a circle. An answer to a question that an earlier answer has since hidden is dropped. It cannot go on deciding what else is asked. The form reacts as it is filled in, and the server decides again when the answers are sent. The two use the same rules, held together by one file of test cases.

title: Running the program
heading: Versions
text: Edit changes a questionnaire's sections, questions, their kinds and options, and when each is asked, with the form as it will be asked shown beneath. Saving changed questions publishes a new version . Earlier versions are never altered. An answer is read against the version it was given to. Reword a question or remove one, and what people answered before still reads as it was asked then. A draft begun under one version is finished under that version. A built-in questionnaire you have edited is yours from then on, and a later release leaves it alone. One you have not touched is brought up to date, as a new version. Versions lists every one, with who published it and what they said had changed

text: Back up the data home, and the database as well if you use PostgreSQL. Evidence files are in the data home under files/ , and the database refers to them. uv run riskwren program export keeps a copy of the program you have shaped. If nobody can sign in, riskwren users adds an administrator or resets a password from the server's own command line. Changes made there are recorded in the history as made at the command line.

title: Configuration
heading: Configuration
text: Configuration This guide is for whoever runs the server. It covers riskwren.toml , environment overrides, the data home, PostgreSQL, running behind a reverse proxy, and the guard on demo installations.

title: Configuration
heading: What is configured where
text: RiskWren keeps two kinds of settings apart. Kind Where it lives Examples How the server runs riskwren.toml and the environment Address, port, database, data home The program and the product's look The database, set in the app or by a program pack Risk categories, appetite, the scoring method, cadences, vocabularies, name, logo, colors This guide is about the first. For the second, see Running the program . The look is the one thing that can live in either place. Most organizations set it in the app. One that needs its brand reproduced exactly can fix it in the file: see [branding] .

title: Configuration
heading: Where the file is found
text: uv run riskwren init writes a commented riskwren.toml in the current directory. Every command looks for the file in this order: The --config FILE option (short form -c ), given before the command. The RISKWREN_CONFIG environment variable. ./riskwren.toml . uv run riskwren --config /etc/riskwren/riskwren.toml doctor Relative paths in the file are resolved against the file's own directory, not the directory you run from. An installation therefore moves as a unit.

title: Configuration
heading: Every section and key
text: The file has five sections. Only the first three matter for a new installation; [sso] and [mail] are optional. A section or key that RiskWren does not know is an error, not something it ignores. Every problem in the file is reported together.

title: Configuration
heading: [branding]
text: Optional. Leave it out and the look is set in the app, under Admin → Appearance , as before. Use this section when the look has to be exact: every color by day and after dark, the official logo files, the brand's typefaces. It is also the way to keep a brand in version control, or to give several installations the same look. What is set here wins over what the app stores, and shows under Admin → Appearance as locked, marked Set in the configuration file . Whatever this section leaves out can still be changed in the app. Nothing here is written to the database, so taking a line out gives that setting back to the app. A change takes effect when the server is restarted. Key Meaning product_name

title: Configuration
heading: Environment overrides
text: Any value can be overridden by an environment variable named RISKWREN_<SECTION>_<KEY> , in capitals. The environment wins over the file. Variable Overrides RISKWREN_SERVER_HOST [server] host RISKWREN_SERVER_PORT [server] port RISKWREN_SERVER_WORKERS [server] workers RISKWREN_SERVER_BASE_URL [server] base_url RISKWREN_SERVER_SESSION_IDLE_HOURS [server] session_idle_hours RISKWREN_SERVER_SESSION_MAX_DAYS [server] session_max_days RISKWREN_DATABASE_URL [database] url RISKWREN_DATA_HOME [data] home RISKWREN_SERVER_PORT=8080 uv run riskwren serve RISKWREN_CONFIG is separate: it names the file itself.

title: Configuration
heading: Secrets are refused in the file
text: riskwren.toml is meant to be safe to read, copy, and keep under version control. RiskWren refuses to start if the file holds a secret: a key that looks like a password, secret, token, or key, or a database address with a password in it. Put secrets in the environment instead. For the database, set the password in PGPASSWORD , or put the whole address, password and all, in RISKWREN_DATABASE_URL .

title: Configuration
heading: The data home
text: The data home is created by init . With the default settings it is ./var . Path Holds The SQLite database When no database address is set brand/ Uploaded logos and the tab icon logs/ The server's log, rotated files/ Evidence files, each stored once under the SHA-256 of its content. Nothing here is served directly exports/ Reserved for exports .riskwren-home A marker that says this directory is a data home Back it up as a whole. With PostgreSQL, back up the database as well. Do not edit its contents by hand. It must be writable by the account that runs the server. Request bodies and tokens are never written to the log.

title: Configuration
heading: Single sign-on
text: You do not need this to use RiskWren. A new installation signs in with an email address and a password that RiskWren keeps, and an evaluation or a small team needs nothing else. Single sign-on is something an administrator adds when the organization wants people to use the account they already have, under its own multi-factor authentication and offboarding. When it is on, it sits beside local accounts and does not replace them. The sign-in page shows the organization's button first, with the password form folded beneath it. An administrator can always sign in with a password, so a provider that is down or misconfigured never locks everyone out. RiskWren speaks OpenID Connect: the authorizati

title: Configuration
heading: What you set, and where
text: What Where The provider's issuer and RiskWren's client ID [sso] in riskwren.toml The client secret An environment variable, RISKWREN_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET unless you name another RiskWren's public address [server] base_url , so the redirect address is always the same Which of the provider's roles or groups give which role here In the app: Admin → Single sign-on The redirect address to give the provider is <base_url>/api/v1/sso/callback . Admin → Single sign-on shows it, before and after you set anything up.

title: Configuration
heading: With Microsoft Entra ID
text: In the Entra admin center, open App registrations → New registration . Name it, choose Accounts in this organizational directory only , and add a Web redirect URI: your base_url followed by /api/v1/sso/callback . From the registration's Overview , copy the Application (client) ID and the Directory (tenant) ID . Under Certificates & secrets , add a client secret and copy its Value . It is shown once. Under App roles , create a role for each kind of access you want to give from Entra ID, for users and groups. The role's Value is what RiskWren sees: for example RiskWren.Admin , RiskWren.Assessor , RiskWren.Security.Leader . Under Enterprise applications , open the same application, then Users a

title: Configuration
heading: With another provider
text: Register RiskWren as a confidential web client with the redirect address above. Set issuer to the address whose /.well-known/openid-configuration the provider serves, and client_id to what it gave you. Have it put a person's groups or roles in a claim, and name that claim in roles_claim (many providers call it groups ). If the provider says email_verified is true for its addresses, leave trust_email as it is.

title: Configuration
heading: Roles from the provider
text: Admin → Single sign-on lists mappings. Each says: everyone the provider gives this value gets this role here. Role here For Works in a unit One unit. Membership grants nothing by itself; it decides what a member sees Steward, Leader One unit, and everything beneath it. A leader's mapping also says what they may accept Assessor, Manager The whole organization, or one unit Auditor, Administrator The whole organization Roles given this way are set again at every sign-in . Take the role away at the provider and it is gone here the next time the person signs in. A shorter session_max_days shortens the wait. Roles given by hand under Admin → People are left alone, and are shown apart from those th

title: Configuration
heading: Who a person is
text: A person is known by the provider's own identifier for them, never by an address alone. The first time someone signs in: if an account here has the address the provider vouches for, the two are joined, and from then on the provider's identifier is what counts; otherwise an account is made for them, with the roles their mappings give, unless create_accounts is false . A disabled account cannot come in through the provider. Signing out of RiskWren does not sign anyone out of the provider.

title: Configuration
heading: Passwords, once it is on
text: With local_sign_in = true , anyone who has a password may still use it. With false , only administrators may. There is no setting that removes the administrator's password, on purpose: it is the way in when the provider cannot be reached.

title: Configuration
heading: Try it on a laptop
text: scripts/dev_identity_provider.py is a stand-in provider for trying this out. It has a fixed list of people and no passwords, and its signing key is published in the file, so it proves nothing and listens only on the machine it runs on. uv run python scripts/dev_identity_provider.py Then set issuer = "http://127.0.0.1:8099" , client_id = "riskwren-dev" , and trust_email = true under [sso] , and start RiskWren with RISKWREN_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET=dev-secret in its environment.

title: Configuration
heading: Scheduled work
text: RiskWren does four things by itself, so that nobody has to remember to. Job How often What it does The calendar Hourly Brings risks up to date when a plan passes its date or an acceptance ends Reminders Hourly Reminds people of what is nearly due, and tells stewards and leaders what stays late. See Reminders Email Every minute Queues notices and daily summaries and sends what is waiting, where email is set up Measures Every six hours Takes the day's snapshot of every measure, for its trend; a later one the same day replaces it Housekeeping Daily Removes run records older than ninety days and sign-ins that were never finished The server runs them while it is up. Nothing needs to be installed

title: Configuration
heading: Email
text: You do not need this to use RiskWren. Notices and reminders are read in the app, under the bell at the top right, and on Home. Email sends the same notices to people's inboxes as well, for organizations that want that. Under [mail] in riskwren.toml , set host and from_address . If the mail server needs a sign-in, set username , and put the password in the RISKWREN_MAIL_PASSWORD environment variable. Set base_url under [server] , so that messages can link back. Restart RiskWren, and run uv run riskwren doctor : it connects and signs in to the mail server, and sends nothing. Send yourself a message from Admin → Operations , or with uv run riskwren mail test you@example.org . Then each person c

title: Configuration
heading: Use PostgreSQL
text: SQLite is the default and needs no setup. Use PostgreSQL when many people will use RiskWren at once or you want more than one server process. The features and the data model are the same on both, and the test suite runs on both. Install the driver, which is optional: `` bash uv sync --extra postgres `` Create an empty database and a role that owns it, with your usual PostgreSQL tools. Set the address in riskwren.toml , without the password: `` toml [database] url = "postgresql+psycopg://riskwren@db.example.org:5432/riskwren" `` Put the password in the environment, then set up and check: `` bash export PGPASSWORD=… uv run riskwren init uv run riskwren doctor `` To move an existing installatio

title: Configuration
heading: Back up and restore
text: uv run riskwren backup /backups/riskwren-2026-12-01.zip backup writes the whole installation to one file: every table, every file the data home stores (evidence, attachments, uploaded logos), and a manifest that counts and fingerprints each of them and says which version of RiskWren took it. It reads everything as of one moment, so the server can go on running and people can go on working while it does. The file must not exist already. It holds everything, so keep it as carefully as the database itself: somewhere other than the server, and encrypted where your other backups are. The data home's exports and logs are not in it: exports can be made again, and logs belong to the machine. To rest

title: Configuration
heading: Move between SQLite and PostgreSQL
text: A backup is the same whichever database it was taken from, so moving is a backup from one and a restore into the other: uv run riskwren backup move.zip # with the old riskwren.toml uv sync --extra postgres export RISKWREN_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://riskwren@db.example.org:5432/riskwren uv run riskwren --config new/riskwren.toml restore move.zip Stop the server before the backup, so that nothing is written after it, and start it on the new configuration once the restore says that everything matches. People stay signed in: their sessions move with everything else.

title: Configuration
heading: Sizing
text: RiskWren was measured with 10,000 records (systems, processes, risks, and controls), on one laptop with 10 cores ( scripts/measure.py , which anyone can run). title: Configuration
heading: Run behind a reverse proxy
text: RiskWren speaks plain HTTP and expects a reverse proxy to terminate TLS in front of it. Keep host = "127.0.0.1" when the proxy is on the same machine. Have the proxy send X-Forwarded-Proto: https . RiskWren marks its session cookie Secure when the request arrived over HTTPS, by that header or directly. Forward the Host header unchanged. Requests that change anything are refused when their origin does not match the host, which is part of the protection against requests from other sites. Requests larger than 32 MB are refused. The app sets its own security headers, including a content security policy with no inline script or style and no third-party origins, so the proxy does not need to add t

title: Configuration
heading: The demo and the network
text: A demo organization signs in anyone who asks as any of its sample people, with no password. So a demo's server listens only on the machine it runs on: serve refuses any other host, and the sample sign-in refuses requests from other machines. If you do want to show a demo to others on a network you trust: uv run riskwren --config demo/riskwren.toml serve --host 0.0.0.0 --demo-on-network Anyone who can reach it can then sign in as the demo's risk manager or administrator. Never do this with a database that holds anything real; a demo database holds nothing that is.

title: Deployment
heading: Deployment
text: Deployment How to run RiskWren for real: in a container, with PostgreSQL, behind a proxy, backed up, and checked before anyone relies on it. Getting started covers trying it on one machine; Configuration covers every setting. The files this guide uses are in the repository's deploy/ folder.

title: Deployment
heading: Choose how to run it
text: For What it takes A container with PostgreSQL ( deploy/compose.yaml ) Most installations A host with Podman or Docker; the proxy in front A service on the host ( deploy/riskwren.service ) Hosts where containers are not used Python 3.12 or later, uv , PostgreSQL, systemd One process with SQLite A small team, or trying it out Nothing more; see Getting started Whichever you choose: put a reverse proxy in front to end TLS, set base_url to the address people use, back up every day, and run riskwren doctor --production before you tell people it is there.

title: Deployment
heading: In a container
text: deploy/Containerfile builds an image that holds RiskWren and nothing else. It runs as a user of its own, keeps its configuration and data home on the volume at /data , and sets the installation up the first time it starts. cp deploy/.env.example deploy/.env # fill it in; keep it out of version control podman compose -f deploy/compose.yaml --env-file deploy/.env up -d --build ( docker compose works the same way.) The compose file runs PostgreSQL 16 beside RiskWren, waits for it to be ready, and publishes RiskWren on 127.0.0.1:8020 only, for the proxy. In deploy/.env : RISKWREN_BASE_URL : the https:// address people use. RISKWREN_DB_PASSWORD : the database's password, made up for this installa

title: Deployment
heading: As a service on the host
text: Install RiskWren into its own environment, and run it under systemd with deploy/riskwren.service : sudo useradd --system --home-dir /var/lib/riskwren --shell /usr/sbin/nologin riskwren sudo install -d -o riskwren -g riskwren -m 0750 /var/lib/riskwren /etc/riskwren sudo UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/riskwren uv sync --frozen --no-dev --extra postgres --no-editable sudo -u riskwren /opt/riskwren/bin/riskwren --config /etc/riskwren/riskwren.toml init sudo cp deploy/riskwren.service /etc/systemd/system/ sudo systemctl enable --now riskwren In /etc/riskwren/riskwren.toml , set the data home to /var/lib/riskwren/var , the database's address, and base_url . Secrets go in /etc/riskwren/env , readable

title: Deployment
heading: Behind a proxy
text: RiskWren speaks plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1 and expects a proxy to end TLS. deploy/Caddyfile does that with a certificate Caddy obtains itself; deploy/nginx.conf does it with yours. Either sends the Host header unchanged and X-Forwarded-Proto: https , so that RiskWren marks its session cookie Secure and checks where each change comes from. The nginx example keeps no access log for reports made without a name. See Run behind a reverse proxy .

title: Deployment
heading: Back it up
text: Take a backup every day, from a scheduled task, and keep the files somewhere other than the server: riskwren backup /backups/riskwren-$(date +%F).zip A backup is taken while the server runs, and restores into SQLite or PostgreSQL alike. Restore one now and then, onto a spare machine, to know that it works. See Back up and restore .

title: Deployment
heading: Check before going live
text: riskwren doctor --production Besides the usual checks (the configuration, the data home, the database and its schema, the history), it checks what matters before real people rely on it, and exits with 1 if anything must be fixed: Check Ready when Address base_url is the https:// address people use Listening The server listens on this machine only, behind the proxy Database for production PostgreSQL, or SQLite with one worker for a small team Backups A backup was taken in the last two days Demo This is not a demo organization Administrators There are two, so that the installation is never left without one Email for production Email is set up, so that reminders reach people Admin → Operations

title: Deployment
heading: Upgrade
text: Back up, then: in a container, build or pull the new image and restart; on the host, update the environment ( uv sync ) and restart the service. Both bring the database up to date as they start. The changelog says what each release changes, and what looks different afterwards.

title: The API
heading: The API
text: API Everything the web app does, it does through a JSON API under /api/v1 . This guide covers how to sign in, how answers and errors are shaped, how lists page, and what routes there are. The exact shape of every request and answer is in the OpenAPI document: openapi.json in this directory, or /api/openapi.json on a running server. This release has no API tokens. A program signs in as an account, with that account's password, and holds a session as a browser does. Tokens scoped to a role arrive with integrations in a later release; see the roadmap . Until 1.0, routes may change between releases. Changes are listed in the changelog .

title: The API
heading: Sign in
text: curl -s -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"email": "you@example.org", "password": "…"}' \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/session The answer describes who you are, and sets a session cookie, riskwren_session : { "data": { "account": {"id": 12, "name": "Your Name", "email": "you@example.org"}, "roles": ["manager"], "permissions": {"…": true}, "units": {"manager": null}, "member_units": [4], "has_password": true, "csrf_token": "…" }, "meta": {} } In units , each scoped role lists the units it covers, or null for the whole organization. GET /api/v1/session returns the same for the session you hold, or 401 if you hold none. DELETE /api/v1/session signs out.

title: The API
heading: Another system: tokens
text: Another system uses the API with a token, made by an administrator under Admin → Other systems , and sent in a header instead of a cookie: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer rwt_…" https://grc.example.org/api/v1/risks?limit=50 A token acts as a role, never as a person: an auditor's reads everything, a manager's runs the program, an assessor's tests and reviews, a steward's works within one unit, and a member's reads what everyone may. A manager's or an assessor's token may be limited to one unit, and a steward's must be. A token is made to read only unless the administrator says otherwise; a change sent with one that may only read is refused with 403. An administrator's token cannot be made.

title: The API
heading: Being told: webhooks
text: An administrator registers a webhook under Admin → Other systems : a name, an https:// address, and what it is told of: * for everything, a family such as issue.* , or an event such as issue.close or risk.assess . The families are risk, control, issue, exception, incident, document, evidence, assessment, third_party, third_party_review, system, process, scope, and agreement. An event's name is what was done, as the history names it. Within a minute of something happening, each webhook that wants it is sent a POST : { "event": "issue.close", "at": "2026-11-28T14:02:11.402Z", "seq": 10422, "record": {"type": "issue", "ref": "ISS-0031", "url": "https://grc.example.org/issues/ISS-0031"} } A mess

title: The API
heading: The contract
text: docs/api-contract.json records every route, its parameters, and the fields its body takes, and which are needed. A release may add to it: a route, an optional parameter, an optional field. A change that would break a client (a route, a parameter, or a field taken away, or one that was optional made needed) fails the build unless it is made on purpose, and is then listed under Breaking in the changelog .

title: The API
heading: Changing things
text: Every request that changes anything ( POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE ) must carry the session's CSRF token in a header: curl -s -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'X-CSRF-Token: …' \ -d '{"name": "Freezer farm", "kind": "device", "criticality": "critical", "org_unit_id": 4}' \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/systems Without it the answer is 403. If the request carries an Origin header, it must match the host, or the request is refused.

title: The API
heading: Editing a record someone else is editing
text: Records carry a version . Send the version you read with a PATCH , and if someone else has changed the record since, the answer is 409 and nothing is saved. Read it again and decide what to do.

title: The API
heading: Answers
text: Every successful answer has the same envelope: {"data": …, "meta": {…}} data is one object or a list. meta carries what is about the answer and not in it: paging for a list, or a count of what else changed. Times are UTC in ISO 8601. Dates with no time, such as a due date, are YYYY-MM-DD .

title: The API
heading: Errors
text: Errors are problem documents ( application/problem+json ): { "type": "about:blank", "title": "Unprocessable Entity", "status": 422, "detail": "The assessment was not recorded.", "errors": [ {"location": ["rationale"], "message": "Say why, in a sentence or two. A rating is a judgment."} ], "instance": "/api/v1/risks/RSK-0002/assessments" } Status Meaning 400 The request could not be carried out as asked 401 Nobody is signed in, or the email address and password do not match 403 You are signed in but may not do this, or the CSRF token is missing. detail says which 404 No such thing, or none that you may see. The two are not told apart 409 A conflict: the record changed since you read it, or th

title: The API
heading: Lists
text: Every list route takes the same parameters: Parameter Meaning q Words to look for in the name, reference, or summary, or in what the record is called in another system unit A unit's id. Includes every unit beneath it sort A field name. Start with - for descending. The default is -updated_at limit How many to return: 50 by default, 200 at most cursor Where to continue from: next_cursor or prev_cursor from the last answer mine true for only the records you are named on Each kind of record adds its own filters, such as standing , residual_rating , and category for risks. The OpenAPI document lists them. A list's meta says where the page sits: {"total": 180, "offset": 0, "next_cursor": "eyJvZmZz

title: The API
heading: Routes
text: Every route requires a signed-in account except those marked public. What a route allows beyond that depends on the record: its unit, its owners, and its visibility. See Running the program .

title: The API
heading: System and session
text: Route What it does GET /health/live · GET /health/ready Whether the server is up, and whether it can serve (public) GET /meta Product name, version, branding, and palettes (public) GET · POST · DELETE /session Who is signed in; sign in; sign out POST /session/password Change your own password GET /sso/start · GET /sso/callback The single sign-on round trip, for a browser (public; 404 unless it is set up) GET · PUT /session/preferences How you want notices by email, where email is set up GET · POST /questionnaires · GET · PATCH /questionnaires/{key} Questionnaires and their versions; a changed document is published as a new version (changing them is for those who run the program) GET · POST /

title: The API
heading: People and units
text: Route What it does GET /accounts · POST /accounts Find people; add an account (admin) GET · PATCH /accounts/{id} One account; change it PUT /accounts/{id}/roles · PUT /accounts/{id}/units Set its roles and units (admin) POST /accounts/{id}/password Set a password for someone (admin) GET /roles The roles and what each allows GET /units · POST /units · GET · PATCH /units/{id} The organization's units POST /imports/units · POST /imports/people Import from CSV, with dry_run (admin)

title: The API
heading: The inventory, risks, and controls
text: {records} is one of processes , systems , third-parties , information , risks , or controls . A record is addressed by its reference, such as SYS-0036 . Route What it does GET /{records} · POST /{records} List; add (a steward of the unit, or a manager) GET · PATCH /{records}/{ref} One record with everything about it; change it. external_refs sets what it is called in other systems PUT /{records}/{ref}/owners Name its owners, delegates, and contacts GET /{records}/{ref}/history Its history POST /{records}/{ref}/links · DELETE /{records}/{ref}/links/{id} Link two inventory records; unlink them

title: The API
heading: What the API will not do
text: It never returns a record you may not see, and never counts one. It never edits an assessment, a control rating, a test result, or an acceptance. Each is superseded by a new one. It never lets a person record or confirm a test result for a control they own, confirm the closure of an issue they own, or decide an exception they asked for. It never imports a rating. A file can say what a risk or a control is, and not how it has been judged. It never changes the history. There is no route that does.
